activities.title: Prefixes un- and re-
parentPrompts: Write "happy" and add "un" to make "unhappy." Say: "un means not." Then write "read" and add "re" to make "reread." Say: "re means again."
Make cards: un (lock, kind, fair, safe) and re (do, tell, play, fill). Have your child read each new word and say what it means.
Play a quick game: you say "not kind" and they say "unkind"; you say "play again" and they say "replay."
Have them write two sentences using one un word and one re word. Check: they can say that un means not and re means again, and decode the new words.

activities.title: Endings -ed and -ing
parentPrompts: Write "jump" and add endings: jumped, jumping. Say each aloud and ask when we use each one. (-ed for something that already happened, -ing for something happening now.)
Read pairs together: walk/walked/walking, help/helped/helping, play/played/playing. Act out the action for each as you say it.
Some verbs change completely in the past. Practice a few: sit - sat, tell - told, hide - hid. Say a sentence with "today I" and have your child say it with "yesterday I."
Have your child write 3 sentences, one with -ed, one with -ing, and one with sat/told/hid. Check: they use the right ending for past and now.

activities.title: Tricky words
parentPrompts: Explain that some words do not follow the usual sounding-out rules. Write these on cards: said, friend, people, because, would, could, only, every.
Say a word and have your child spell it aloud, look at the card, and trace each letter with a finger. Point out the tricky part (for example, the "ai" in said or the "ie" in friend).
Play "memory flash": show a card for 3 seconds, hide it, and have your child write the word. Then check it against the card.
Pick two words that were hard. Write each one three times and use it in a sentence. Check: they can read and spell at least 6 of the 8 words.

activities.title: Read smooth and understand
materials: a book or passage at your child's reading level
parentPrompts: Choose a short passage of about 5 to 8 sentences your child has not read before. Have them read it aloud once. Note any words that stop them.
Ask them to read it again. If a word does not make sense, say: "Go back and try again." Show them how to reread the sentence to check.
Ask 3 questions: Who or what is it about? What happened? Why do you think so? Have them find the answer in the text.
Compare the two reads: Which sounded smoother? Check: the second read is smoother, and they can fix a mistake by rereading.

activities.title: Fix and publish my story
materials: the story your child wrote in the first week, or a new one
parentPrompts: Read the earlier story aloud together. Ask: "What do you like about it? What could we add?"
Revising: add one detail about a sound, a smell, or a feeling. Use the colored pencil so the new part stands out.
Editing: check capital letters at the start of each sentence, end marks, and spelling of tricky words. Use the word lists from earlier lessons.

Copy the final story neatly onto a clean page and add a picture. Have your child read it aloud to someone. Check: the story has a beginning, middle, and end, and the child can name one thing they changed.

activities.title: Add and regroup
materials: base-ten blocks or paper strips and squares
parentPrompts: Build 38 and 27. Ask: "How many ones in all?" (15.) Trade 10 ones for 1 ten.
Count the tens: 3 + 2 + 1 (the new ten) = 6 tens. So 38 + 27 = 65.
Try 46 + 18 and 29 + 34 with blocks. Ask your child to explain the trade each time.
Check: they can explain why 10 ones become 1 ten.

activities.title: Subtract two-digit numbers
materials: base-ten blocks or paper strips and squares
parentPrompts: Build 52 with 5 tens and 2 ones. Ask: "Can we take away 7 ones?" Trade 1 ten for 10 ones, so now there are 4 tens and 12 ones.
Take away 27 (2 tens, 7 ones). What is left? (25.)
Try 80 - 35 and 73 - 28. Have your child build, trade, and explain.
Check: they use a trade when needed and can write the answer correctly.

activities.title: Adding bigger numbers
materials: base-ten blocks or paper hundreds, tens and ones
parentPrompts: Build 245 and 130. Add the hundreds (2 + 1 = 3 hundreds), tens (4 + 3 = 7 tens), and ones (5 + 0 = 5): 375.
Try 400 + 250 and 326 - 100, then something with a trade like 168 + 47 (the ones make a ten).
Draw a quick picture for each problem using squares for hundreds, lines for tens, and dots for ones.
Check: they can add and subtract within 1000 using hundreds, tens, and ones.

activities.title: Two-step story problems
parentPrompts: Read: "Ana had 24 stickers. She gave 9 to her friend and found 6 more. How many does she have now?" Solve one step at a time: 24 - 9 = 15, then 15 + 6 = 21.
Have your child draw a quick picture or bar for each step and write number sentences.
Make up another with real items at home, such as books on a shelf or apples in a bowl.
Check: they solve each step in order and say what the answer means.

activities.title: Explain why it works
parentPrompts: Pick a problem like 47 + 25. Have your child solve it any way they like.
Ask: "Why does your way work?" Prompt them to use tens and ones to explain, for example: "40 + 20 is 60, 7 + 5 is 12, and 60 + 12 is 72."
Try a different way together (such as making a ten or counting up) and compare the two.
Check: they can explain a strategy in their own words using place value.

activities.title: Some changes cannot be undone
parentPrompts: Show a slice of bread. Ask your child to describe it: soft, pale, bendy.
An adult toasts it while the child stays back from the hot toaster. Look at the toast and describe it: hard, golden, crisp.
Ask: "Can we turn the toast back into soft bread?" (No.) Talk about how heat caused a change that cannot be reversed.
Check: they say some changes caused by heating cannot be undone.

activities.title: Can it change back?
materials: cards with changes: ice melting, bread toasting, water freezing, candle wax melting, pancake batter cooking, butter melting
parentPrompts: Write each change on a card. Make two piles: Can change back and Cannot change back.
Talk about each one and why. (Do not burn anything. Just discuss.)
Ask: "What do the reversible changes have in common?" (Usually melting or freezing.)
Check: they can give a reason for each sort using what they learned.

activities.title: Material engineer challenge
materials: a choice of materials: paper, foil, cloth, plastic, cardboard
parentPrompts: Challenge: build a small shelter for the toy that keeps it dry when you sprinkle water on it.
Before building, have your child choose materials and explain why, based on earlier tests.
Test it by sprinkling a little water on the roof. Did it work? What would you change?
Check: they pick materials for a reason and use test results to improve their design.

activities.title: Continents and oceans
parentPrompts: Show the globe. Explain that most of Earth is covered by water. The big land areas are continents. The big bodies of water are oceans.
Name the 7 continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Name the 5 oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic.
Trace a world map with your child and color each continent a different color. Color the oceans blue.
Ask: "Which continent do we live on? Which ocean is closest?" Check: they can find their continent and name at least two oceans.

activities.title: Make a treasure map
parentPrompts: Hide a small object in the house or yard. Make a map of the path, with symbols, a key, and a compass rose.
Write 3 clues that use directions, such as "Walk north past the tree" or "Turn east at the fence."
Have a family member follow the map to find the treasure. Then swap roles.
Check: they use a map key, symbols, and directions clearly enough that someone else can follow.
